questions.prompt: Which word can replace "who" in: "The police arrested the man who was cutting the trees."?
questions.explanation: "That" can replace "who" and "which": the man that was cutting the trees. "Which" cannot refer to a person, and the common trap "what" is a question word, never a relative pronoun after a noun.

questions.prompt: Complete: "This exam is ___ the one we did last month." (difficult)
questions.explanation: "Difficult" is a long adjective, so it takes "more" and "than": more difficult than. "Difficulter" adds -er to a long adjective, "as" is the word of equality, and "the most" is the superlative, which never takes "than".

questions.prompt: Complete: "In July, Kairouan is ___ than Tabarka." (hot)
questions.explanation: "Hot" ends with one vowel + one consonant, so the consonant doubles before -er: hotter. "Hoter" is the classic spelling slip, "more" is only for long adjectives, and "hottest" is the superlative.

options.text: It is the most beautiful house in town.
It is the most beautifulest house in town.
It is the more beautiful house in town.
It is most beautiful house in town.

questions.explanation: "Beautiful" is long, so its superlative is "the most beautiful". "The most beautifulest" uses "the most" and -est together, "the more" is a comparative, and "most beautiful house" alone forgets "the".

questions.prompt: Rim gets 10 dinars a week. Her brother gets 10 dinars a week, too. Complete: "Rim gets ___ her brother."
questions.explanation: The two amounts are equal, so we use as much + noun + as: as much pocket money as. "More … than" says Rim gets more, which is false; "than" never closes an equality; and "much pocket money as" forgets the first "as".

options.text: The girl who she won the race is my cousin.
The girl which won the race is my cousin.
The girl won the race is my cousin.
The girl who won the race is my cousin.

questions.explanation: "Who" refers to the girl and is already the subject of "won": the girl who won the race. Adding "she" gives "won" two subjects, "which" cannot refer to a person, and without a relative pronoun the two sentences are not joined.
